title: Access and refresh tokens
idea: An access token is short-lived and travels with each request. A refresh token lives longer and is used to get a new access token.

analogy.text: A day pass and a membership card. The day pass opens every door but expires tonight; the membership card buys a new day pass at the desk.
analogy.breaks: Unlike a card, the server keeps a copy of the refresh token.

points: The access token goes with every request, in the `accessToken` cookie.
It expires quickly, so a stolen copy stops working soon.
The refresh token lasts longer, and the server saves a copy on the user.
The refresh route matches it to the saved copy, issuing a new access token.

hero.title: From login to refresh to logout

messages.label: POST /auth/login
messages.note: At login the password travels once. The API checks it against the stored hash.

messages.label: save refreshToken
messages.note: The API signs an access token and a refresh token, and saves the refresh token on the user.

messages.label: set both cookies
messages.note: Both tokens return in `httpOnly` cookies. The browser stores them; page JavaScript cannot read them.

messages.label: GET /auth/current-user
messages.note: Each request carries the access token. The API verifies its signature and expiry.

messages.label: 401 Unauthorized
messages.note: Later the access token has expired and verification fails. The user does not have to log in again.

messages.label: POST /auth/refresh-token
messages.note: The client calls the refresh route. The refresh token travels in its cookie.

messages.label: check saved copy
messages.note: The API verifies the refresh token and checks it against the copy saved on the user.

messages.label: new access token
messages.note: A match earns a new access token. The user never typed the password again.

messages.label: logout: clear copy
messages.note: On logout the API clears the saved copy. That refresh token can no longer be exchanged.

code.title: Two tokens, two lifetimes
code.caption: Both are JWTs with different secrets and lifetimes. The project reads them from `.env`; the next page builds them as model methods.

walk.text: Two different secrets. A token signed with one fails verification with the other.
The access token gets a short life.
The refresh token gets a long one: seven days.
`exp - iat` is the lifetime in seconds. Compare the two.
A refresh token offered as an access token fails: wrong secret.
Verified with its own secret, the refresh token yields its `_id`.

pitfalls: Sign refresh tokens with a different secret, so one cannot pass as the other.
Logout must clear the saved refresh token; clearing cookies alone leaves a stolen copy usable.
Prefer `httpOnly` cookies to `localStorage`: any script on the page can read `localStorage`.

quiz.why: The secret is right but `expiresIn: -1` puts the expiry in the past. `jwt.verify` throws `jwt expired`; the client would now call the refresh route.

takeaway: Short-lived access tokens do the work; a long-lived refresh token renews them.

starters: Why not use one token with a long expiry?
What can an attacker do with a stolen refresh token?
Why are the tokens stored in cookies and not in localStorage?
